slides.title: Classifying rejection from kidney biopsy RNA
paragraphs: This project asks a specific question: once a kidney transplant biopsy has been collected, can its molecular measurements classify the rejection diagnosis recorded for that tissue?
actions: Pause after the research question, then move to the biopsy diagram.

slides.title: Kidney biopsy and transplant rejection
paragraphs: A kidney transplant gives a person a kidney from a donor. The recipient's immune system can recognize that kidney as foreign and attack it. That immune response is what we mean here by rejection.

A biopsy is a small tissue sample taken from the kidney. Follow the two branches on the slide. A specialist can examine thin sections under a microscope for patterns of injury and inflammation. Histology means studying tissue in this way. The study records a diagnosis for each specimen.
The other branch contains molecular measurements from biopsy tissue. Those measurements become the model inputs. The recorded diagnosis supplies the answer used to train and evaluate the classifier.

A transplant pathology or molecular laboratory team could use this research comparison to study agreement between measurements and recorded diagnoses. The tissue has already been collected, and the question concerns that specimen at that time.
actions: Trace the tissue sample into the microscope and molecular-measurement branches.
Point to the research-use caption when explaining the comparison.
visible_cues: Rejection: immune attack on a donor kidney
Biopsy tissue: a small tissue sample
Research use: compare measurements with recorded diagnoses

slides.title: Recorded diagnoses
paragraphs: The study records four diagnoses. Antibody-mediated rejection involves antibodies, which are proteins made by the immune system. T-cell-mediated rejection involves T cells, a type of immune cell. Mixed rejection includes both processes.

For this project's main question, those three categories all count as rejection. The fourth category, no rejection, supplies the comparison group. No rejection does not necessarily mean the tissue is healthy. It means the recorded diagnosis is outside those rejection categories.
The classifier therefore answers a two-category question: rejection or no rejection. The original four diagnoses remain available so we can later examine which kinds of rejection it misses.
actions: Read down the diagnosis table, then point to the common rejection label.
visible_cues: T-cell-mediated: T cells are immune cells
No rejection does not necessarily mean healthy
Three rejection diagnoses become one rejection label

slides.title: Measuring RNA in biopsy tissue
paragraphs: RNA includes the messages cells make when genes are expressed. Measuring these messages gives us information about which genes are active and how much of their RNA is present in the tissue sample.
An assay is a laboratory test. This study uses NanoString nCounter with the B-HOT panel. A panel is the fixed list of molecules the assay is designed to measure.
Molecular probes recognize selected RNA molecules. Identifying barcodes allow the instrument to count their signals. Each named measurement becomes a number in the specimen's record.

For example, IFNG is one of the named RNA measurements. In the public specimen we'll follow through the application, its raw count is four. The diagram explains how RNA becomes a count. The IFNG example shows the kind of number the analysis actually receives.
actions: Follow RNA, probe recognition, barcode counting, and the IFNG example in order.
Point to the IFNG count of 4. Treat the assay diagram as an illustration.
visible_cues: RNA: gene messages in the tissue
Probes recognize selected RNA; barcodes identify counted signals
Panel: a fixed list of measurements

slides.title: The measurements used by the model
paragraphs: Each specimen has 770 measurements. Of these, 758 describe RNA signals that will become model inputs. Some measure viral RNA, so the full set includes more than human genes.
The remaining 12 are housekeeping measurements. They provide a reference level for preparing the counts. After that preparation, the model receives the 758 other measurements.
Assay documentation sometimes calls a molecule a target because a probe is designed to recognize it. Here I'll use measurement for an input and recorded rejection for the outcome we want to classify.
These counts describe a piece of tissue. A larger count can reflect greater activity within cells, a different mixture of cells, or both.
actions: Use the 758 plus 12 breakdown to distinguish inputs from reference measurements.
Define molecular target once, then use measurement in the remaining explanation.
visible_cues: Molecular target: the molecule a probe recognizes
Housekeeping measurements prepare the inputs, then are removed
Counts reflect cell activity and the mixture of cells

sources.label: Bruker: nCounter technology and molecular barcodes

slides.title: One row describes one biopsy specimen
paragraphs: One row represents one biopsy specimen. Its public specimen ID connects the raw-count file with the diagnosis record. The example ID, GSM6510425, identifies the same specimen in both places. It is simply a way to match the records.
The data checks account for all 1,395 specimens. All are included, with no exclusions. The checks also found no duplicate normalized measurement profiles across the data splits.

The row keeps measurements separate from information used to describe or evaluate the specimen. The model receives the prepared RNA measurements. The specimen ID, diagnosis, and cohort name stay outside its predictors.
These are counts of specimens. The available records do not establish the number of unique patients or centers, so 1,395 specimens cannot be described as 1,395 independent patients.
actions: Point to the public specimen ID above the diagram, then follow how it matches the count record with the diagnosis record.
Point to the fields excluded from predictors.
visible_cues: Public specimen ID GSM6510425 joins counts and diagnosis
No duplicate normalized profiles across splits
Measurements are inputs; ID, diagnosis, and cohort are separate
Specimen count does not establish unique patient count

slides.title: Preparing counts for the model
paragraphs: The raw counts need consistent preparation. We first add one to each count and take its base-two logarithm. Adding one lets a zero count be transformed. The logarithm compresses the range of values.
The example makes that arithmetic visible. IFNG has a raw count of four. Four plus one is five, and the base-two logarithm of five is about 2.322.

Next, apply the same transformation to the specimen's 12 housekeeping measurements and take their average. For this specimen, that reference average is about 7.900. Subtracting it from 2.322 gives a prepared IFNG value of minus 5.578.

We repeat that subtraction for each of the 758 RNA measurements. Each becomes a value relative to the reference level in its own specimen. The 12 housekeeping measurements have now done their job and are removed from the model inputs.

This calculation uses only the specimen being scored. It needs neither its diagnosis nor counts from other specimens. Additional preparation that learns from data, such as scaling the inputs for logistic regression, is fitted on training specimens only and then reused unchanged.
actions: Walk down the example calculation, including the plus one before the logarithm.
Point to the 12-reference average and the final 758 inputs.
Separate the within-specimen calculation from later training-only learned preparation.
visible_cues: Later learned transforms fitted on training data only

sources.label: Demo behavior and exact invalid-input response

slides.title: Development and evaluation specimens
paragraphs: The study authors supplied two groups, also called cohorts. The discovery cohort contains 1,050 specimens. The technical-validation cohort contains 345. This project preserves that original division.

Within discovery, a saved split assigns 787 specimens to training and 263 to screening. The split keeps the original four diagnosis proportions similar. Training fits the model. Screening compares candidates and chooses the score threshold used to make a rejection flag.

The separate 345 specimens then evaluate the selected procedure. All four comparison models use those same evaluation rows. The selected fitted model and its threshold remain together, without refitting before that evaluation.

These roles explain which data influence each decision. They also define the limit of the separation. The authors call the second group technical validation, but the available records do not establish that it contains entirely different patients or centers.
actions: Trace 1,050 into 787 training and 263 screening, then point to the separate 345 branch.
Use the source term technical validation and state the patient/center limit.
visible_cues: Freeze the fitted model and its threshold before evaluation

slides.title: Four model comparisons
paragraphs: The comparison begins with a constant model. It gives every specimen the same score, equal to the rejection fraction in training. It tells us what happens without using the RNA measurements at all.
The IFNG model uses just the one measurement we've already seen. It tests how much information that single measurement provides.
Logistic regression combines the measurements using learned weights. Regularization restricts the size of those weights, helping the model avoid fitting the training data too closely.
CatBoost combines many decision trees. A tree asks a sequence of questions about measurement values, and the combined trees can represent more complicated relationships.

All four comparisons use the same specimens and preparation. That lets us ask whether the additional measurements help, and whether CatBoost improves enough over the simpler logistic model to justify the added complexity.
actions: Move through the four models in the displayed order.
Finish at the shared rows and preparation cue.
visible_cues: Constant: same training rejection fraction for everyone
Logistic regression: weighted combination; regularization restricts weights

slides.title: Turning a score into a rejection flag
paragraphs: A model produces a score. A threshold turns that score into a flag: scores at or above the threshold count as rejection. A recorded rejection below it becomes a missed rejection. A no-rejection specimen at or above it becomes a false flag.
For this experiment, screening chooses a threshold that retains at least 90 percent of recorded rejection cases, then makes as few false flags as possible.

The selected CatBoost model keeps its threshold of approximately 0.876588 for evaluation and for the application. The 90 percent rule is an experimental choice, not a clinical requirement or a guaranteed result elsewhere.
Choosing a threshold also does not establish that the score is a reliable individual probability. The application therefore calls it a model score.
actions: Point to the threshold before naming misses and false flags.
Point to the frozen threshold and the model-score label.
visible_cues: Score at or above threshold becomes rejection flag
Screening rule: retain at least 90%, then minimize false flags
Model score; probability calibration is a separate question

slides.title: Several measurements reduced false flags
paragraphs: Here are the results on the 345 evaluation specimens. The two colors distinguish the errors: how many of the 169 recorded rejection specimens were missed, and how many of the 176 no-rejection specimens were falsely flagged? Keep those two denominators in mind as we compare the models.

The constant model flags every specimen at its fixed threshold. It misses zero of 169 rejection specimens, but falsely flags all 176 of 176 no-rejection specimens. That shows why detection alone cannot tell us whether a model is useful.
The IFNG-only model misses 14 of 169 rejection specimens and falsely flags 75 of 176 no-rejection specimens. It detects many rejection cases, but it also produces many false flags.
The full-panel logistic model misses 33 of 169 rejection specimens and makes eight false flags among 176 no-rejection specimens. CatBoost misses 25 of 169 and also makes eight false flags among 176.

Compared with IFNG, CatBoost makes 67 fewer false flags but misses 11 more rejection cases. Both parts of that tradeoff matter. The threshold rule chosen in development leads to different error counts in this evaluation group.

Compared with logistic regression, CatBoost detects eight more rejection specimens with the same false-flag count. Combining measurements helps reduce false flags here. The smaller difference between the two full-panel models needs closer examination before we treat it as a dependable advantage.
actions: Read the rejection and no-rejection denominators before the chart.
Explain the constant-model caption, then the IFNG bars at the bottom, logistic bars in the middle, and CatBoost bars at the top.
Pause on the IFNG tradeoff and the eight-case difference from logistic.
visible_cues: CatBoost versus IFNG: 67 fewer false flags, 11 more misses

slides.title: Most CatBoost misses were T-cell rejection
paragraphs: The original four diagnoses help us examine those 25 CatBoost misses. It misses six of 56 antibody-mediated rejection specimens, 18 of 95 T-cell-mediated specimens, and one of 18 mixed specimens.

T-cell-mediated rejection accounts for most misses. It is also the largest rejection group, which is why the denominators remain visible. About 19 percent of that group was missed, compared with about 11 percent of the antibody-mediated group. The mixed group has only 18 specimens, so its single miss gives limited evidence about what to expect elsewhere.

Across all rejection specimens, the model detects 144 of 169, or 85.2 percent. This fraction is called sensitivity. On screening, it detected 157 of 174, or 90.2 percent. The evaluation result falls below the 90 percent used to select the threshold.

That shortfall shows why a screening rule cannot guarantee the same result on new specimens. These are disagreements with recorded diagnoses. Resolving an individual disagreement would require tissue and clinical-record review, which this analysis does not provide.
actions: Point to each miss count with its denominator.
Compare 144 / 169 with 157 / 174 and make the shortfall explicit.
Keep the recorded-diagnosis qualification tied to the error counts.
visible_cues: Errors are disagreements with recorded diagnoses

sources.label: Errors by original diagnosis and screening comparison

slides.title: The advantage over logistic regression is uncertain
paragraphs: CatBoost detects eight more of the 169 rejection specimens than logistic regression, and each makes eight false flags among 176 no-rejection specimens. How much confidence should we place in that difference?

Resampling repeatedly draws from these specimens, allowing a specimen to appear more than once. Both models use the same draws. The 95 percent interval for their detection difference includes zero. This holds the models fixed and does not establish patient independence.

A second check repeats development with 20 saved discovery splits. Each repetition separates fitting, screening, and assessment. The selection rule chooses CatBoost in 13 repetitions and logistic regression in seven.

Those repetitions reuse many specimens. They show how model choice varies with the split, rather than providing 20 independent studies. The demonstration retains the frozen CatBoost model. Logistic regression remains a credible simpler comparison for the next cohort.
actions: Point first to the eight-case difference, then to the sentence stating that the interval includes zero.
Move to the separate 13-of-20 and 7-of-20 follow-up.
State that repetitions overlap before drawing the model-choice conclusion.
visible_cues: Eight fewer misses out of 169; same 8 / 176 false flags
Evaluation resampling keeps fitted models fixed
Keep logistic regression as a simpler alternative

slides.title: Training and serving share the same preprocessing
paragraphs: The software uses the same preparation code during training and when it scores an incoming file. A CSV can enter through the command line or the web application. Both routes check the required measurements, normalize each specimen, and call the configured model.

The response contains the specimen ID, model score, frozen threshold, rejection flag, and model version. The version identifies which saved model produced the result. The flag records whether its score crossed the threshold.

The service loads the project-controlled model. A caller can submit counts but cannot upload a replacement model. Missing measurements, duplicate names, negative counts, and non-finite values cause explicit errors instead of a score.

The score label matters here. The reliability analysis did not establish trustworthy individual probabilities across the score range, so the application presents a model score alongside the threshold that gives the flag its meaning.
actions: Trace the incoming CSV through the shared preparation steps and the frozen model.
Point to the response fields, then the text listing failures that stop scoring.
Keep model version, score, and threshold distinct.
visible_cues: Training and serving share preparation code
Response: ID, score, threshold, flag, version
Missing, duplicate, negative, or non-finite values cause an error
Callers submit counts, not model files

paragraphs: This is the public discovery-screen specimen we've followed, GSM6510425, recorded as no rejection. It demonstrates software behavior. The evaluation results came from the separate technical-validation group.

I'll request its research score. The page identifies the model version and the frozen threshold, approximately 0.876588. This specimen receives a score of about 0.275, below the threshold, so its rejection flag is false.

Under 'Follow the specimen,' IFNG has the raw count of four we saw earlier. Its transformed count is 2.322. Subtracting the housekeeping average of 7.900 gives minus 5.578. The same operation prepares all 758 inputs. This calculation lets us inspect preparation. The model then combines the prepared measurements to produce its score.

Now I'll try the incomplete file. It contains the same public example with IFNG removed. The application clears the earlier result and identifies the missing measurement. The error message calls it an assay target. No score is returned, and the user can correct the file before submitting it again.

slides.title: The service reproduces all 345 saved scores
paragraphs: The checks focus on failures that could change a result. Reordering valid columns must preserve the score. Missing or duplicate measurements must fail. If the model and its expected input definition are incompatible, the service must stop the model from loading.

The September seventeenth local record reports 94 passing tests. A real HTTP comparison checked all 345 evaluation specimens. The API, command line, and saved results agreed within the required tolerance of one times ten to the minus twelve, with identical flags.
The local research container also served the public examples and rejected the invalid one. These checks establish software consistency. The cloud deployment remains deferred.
actions: Point to the three failure checks before the 345-score comparison.
Identify the dated check record and the required agreement tolerance.

slides.title: The result applies to one deposited study
paragraphs: The evidence supports agreement with recorded diagnoses in one deposited study. Patient and center independence remain unverified. The available assay groups are also linked to cohort membership, so their effects cannot be cleanly separated from differences between the specimen groups.
The software checks that a file contains the expected measurements and usable numbers. Those checks do not establish that the laboratory assay passed its quality controls.

The next useful step is a new cohort with patient and center identifiers and documented assay quality. Specify the models and thresholds before evaluation, and retain logistic regression in that fixed comparison.
That would test whether these error counts persist when the study setting changes. Any further calibration or model changes would need their own development and evaluation.
actions: Pair each current limitation with the information required in a new cohort.
Describe the new-cohort comparison as proposed work.
visible_cues: Patient and center identifiers unavailable for independence checks
Assay groups linked to cohort membership
Numeric checks do not establish laboratory quality

slides.title: Molecular counts can classify recorded rejection
paragraphs: The finding is a concrete tradeoff. The frozen CatBoost model missed 25 of 169 rejection specimens and made eight false flags among 176 no-rejection specimens. Its advantage over logistic regression remains uncertain.
The project also provides shared prediction code, explicit input errors, and saved evidence that another person can inspect and reproduce. The next step is a fixed comparison on a new cohort.
Zhang and colleagues supplied the public study. AI assisted with preparing this presentation, and its quantitative claims trace to the project's saved runs. Thank you.

backups.title: Backup: complete primary comparison
paragraphs: This table keeps the four models on the same 345 evaluation specimens. Miss counts use the 169 recorded rejection specimens. False-flag counts use the 176 recorded no-rejection specimens. Sensitivity is the fraction of rejection specimens flagged, and specificity is the fraction of no-rejection specimens left unflagged.

CatBoost has 85.2 percent sensitivity and 95.5 percent specificity, compared with 80.5 and 95.5 percent for logistic regression. IFNG detects a larger fraction of rejection specimens, at 91.7 percent sensitivity, but its specificity is 57.4 percent. The constant baseline flags everyone.

ROC-AUC describes how well scores rank rejection above no rejection across possible thresholds. CatBoost has ROC-AUC 0.969, logistic regression 0.956, IFNG 0.842, and the constant baseline 0.500. The error counts describe each model at its frozen threshold.
actions: Answer the requested metric question by pointing to its table column. Keep both class denominators visible.

backups.title: Backup: normalization and threshold selection
paragraphs: For each specimen, the normalized measurement equals log base two of its raw count plus one, minus the mean log base two of the 12 housekeeping counts plus one. Every required measurement must be present. The reference comes from that specimen alone.

Logistic regression also scales its inputs using quantities learned only from training rows. Its regularization setting is C equals 0.1. The selected CatBoost model uses 300 trees with depth four and learning rate 0.04. These settings describe the saved comparison.

The screening rule chooses thresholds retaining at least 90 percent of screening rejection specimens and minimizing false flags. Both models detected 157 of 174 rejection specimens. Among 89 no-rejection specimens, CatBoost falsely flagged five and logistic regression six. This screening comparison selected CatBoost.

The frozen service flags scores at or above 0.8765880870219778. It retains the fitted model used to choose that threshold. Refitting the model would require a compatible threshold-selection procedure.
actions: Use the formula for preparation questions, the model-settings text for configuration questions, and the screening counts for selection questions.

backups.title: Backup: ranking does not guarantee calibrated scores
paragraphs: This reliability plot groups evaluation specimens into ten fixed score ranges. For each range, it compares the average model score with the fraction of specimens recorded as rejection. Agreement with the diagonal would mean that those two quantities match in that range.

In the highlighted range from 0.8 to 0.9, the mean score is 0.847. Seven of the 16 specimens have recorded rejection, or 43.8 percent. The displayed 95 percent interval for that fraction runs from 23.1 to 66.8 percent. The group is small, and this range was highlighted after inspecting the plot.

A model can rank specimens well without producing reliable probabilities in each score range. No calibration model was fitted on the evaluation data. The application therefore calls its output a model score.
actions: Keep the bin count visible when describing a gap.
Do not interpret 0.876588 as a proven 87.7 percent individual risk.

backups.title: Backup: subtype follow-up retained the binary service
paragraphs: This follow-up compared models trained on the four diagnoses with the original model trained on rejection versus no rejection. The table converts each result to the same any-rejection question, using discovery-selected rules, so the displayed error counts are comparable.

The binary CatBoost benchmark misses 25 of 169 rejection specimens with eight false flags among 176 no-rejection specimens. Four-class CatBoost misses 29 with eight false flags, and four-class logistic misses 28 with ten false flags. The separate antibody and T-cell component models miss 24 with 15 false flags. That last approach finds one additional rejection case while adding seven false flags.

The four-class logistic model correctly identifies ten of 18 mixed diagnoses and makes five false mixed calls among 327 non-mixed specimens. That is a separate subtype question from the binary counts in the table.
The follow-up supplied no reason to replace the frozen binary service. Because this evaluation cohort had already been examined, these findings require confirmation in a new cohort.
actions: Explain the any-rejection conversion before comparing table rows.
Point to the separate mixed-diagnosis sentence only when discussing subtype recognition.

backups.title: Backup: study, assay and deployment limits
paragraphs: The recorded metadata does not confirm patient or transplant-center independence. Biopsy-level resampling may therefore give uncertainty intervals that are too narrow if some specimens are related.

The software checks required measurements and usable numeric counts. The project did not independently repeat laboratory quality checks such as control-probe or imaging checks. Assay compatibility and completed laboratory quality checks remain requirements for a meaningful input.

The score reliability analysis does not establish trustworthy individual probabilities, so the service labels its output a model score. The local research container has been tested. Cloud deployment remains deferred.
actions: Answer the relevant row of the limitations table, then use the specimen-resampling note if asked about uncertainty.

backups.title: Backup: sources and contributions
paragraphs: Zhang and colleagues supplied the public study and the GSE212160 deposit. This project uses their raw measurements for its own binary comparison. It does not reconstruct the authors' published classifier.

The project provides its own saved model runs, shared software, and a tested local demonstration. Configurations, input hashes, reports, and source code allow another person to inspect the quantitative claims.

The presentation guide draws on Bourne for audience and rehearsal, Kosslyn and colleagues for presentation flaws, Garner and Alley for connecting slide statements to evidence, and Rougier and colleagues for clear figures. AI assisted with preparing this presentation.
